sources.title: How to write your personal statement: 2026 entry onwards (UCAS)
sources.governs: All UCAS statements (main and, by Durham's rule, the substitute)
sources.notes: Full page fetched. Q1 guidance invites career talk, which disagrees with lse-ps (LSE governs Q1 of the main statement). Says there is no 'wrong' question for a piece of information, so the reviewer must not penalise placement between Q2 and Q3.
extracts: Each answer will have a minimum character count of 350 characters
Admissions staff will still review your personal statement as a whole, so remember not to repeat information
You can use the 4,000 character count limit across all answers in any way you choose
There's no 'wrong' place to include information in your answers
Universities and colleges want to see you have done your research
If you already have a particular profession in mind you could talk about how you'll use this to launch your career.
Universities and colleges will see your grades elsewhere on your application so don't waste time talking about these.
the key thing here is for you to reflect on your experiences and the skills gained relevant to your chosen course.

sources.title: A guide to using AI and ChatGPT with your personal statement (UCAS)
sources.governs: All UCAS statements
sources.notes: Full page fetched. Permits AI for ideas, structure and readability; submitting AI-generated text could be considered cheating. Contains the declaration wording (also on ucas-declaration).
extracts: Generating (and then copying, pasting and submitting) all or a large part of your personal statement from an AI tool such as ChatGPT, and presenting it as your own words, could be considered cheating by universities and colleges and could affect your chances of an offer.
When you complete your application, you now have to declare that your personal statement hasn't been copied or provided from another source, including artificial intelligence software.
If UCAS software detects elements of a personal statement that are similar to others, the universities or colleges it is intended for may be notified.

sources.title: Personal statement (LSE undergraduate admissions)
sources.governs: Main statement (LSE is the priority and strictest lens)
sources.notes: Full page fetched. Governs the main statement. New vs search capture: LSE expects the space to be fully used and spelling/grammar checked; includes a worked poor example ('dreamed of coming to LSE since I was young', naming LSE, listing IB subjects, more about football than the subject).
extracts: At least 80% of the personal statement should emphasise your interest in the programme you are applying for with evidence of your critical engagement with the subject and your super-curricular activity.
For Question 1 you should avoid discussing your future career plans.
For Question 3 applicants are encouraged to use this space to expand on critical reflections already covered in Questions 1 and 2.
Writing the minimum of 350 characters for Question 3 is entirely acceptable.
We expect that your submitted personal statement is structured and coherent and that you fully utilise the space available on your UCAS application form.
We expect that you have checked spelling, punctuation, and grammar and that your Personal Statement flows in a logical order.

We reserve the right to reject your application where it has been found that a statement has significant similarities to a previous submission or has been created with the use of Artificial Intelligence (using tools such as ChatGPT).
We do not encourage applicants to use generative Artificial Intelligence tools to create their personal statement as they do not produce high-quality personal statements and may lead to rejection.
When assessing your personal statement our Admissions Selectors will look at how well your academic interests align with the LSE programme.
If you are applying to one of these programmes, you are advised to give equal weighting to each subject in your statement.
a statement weighted towards only one aspect of the programme will be significantly less competitive.

Our Selectors look for students who can best reflect on the experiences and academic ideas they have encountered through the opportunities available to them, not those who have had the best opportunities.
I have always dreamed of coming to LSE since I was young.
This brief example of a personal statement is poor.

The applicant has specifically mentioned LSE, which is likely to be unattractive to their other choices, and has wasted space listing their International Baccalaureate subjects, which would be shown in the qualifications section.
this student has spent more time talking about football than about history.

sources.title: Writing a Personal Statement (Durham University)
sources.governs: Durham substitute statement (Economics)
sources.notes: Full page fetched. Own views over description; three questions; 350 min.
extracts: The personal statement can be a maximum of 4000 characters in length (including spaces), and each question will require a minimum of 350 characters.
Tell us why you're interested in studying it, and identify one or two stand out areas to talk about in detail.
We want to hear what your thoughts are about your subject and not just a description of something you've read - we want to hear what you think and not just what you've been told or read.
Do you agree or disagree with particular viewpoints?
Avoid using lists - tell us why something you've read or something you've done makes us a good student, rather than providing a long list of things that doesn't spell out your strengths.
Don't waste characters!
You only have 4000 so don't include things like lists of your qualifications - we can see those in the qualifications section of your application already.
